title: 7 things to keep an eye on during election night
text: Donald Trump is trying to break through Hillary Clinton's blue wall, while Clinton is counting on a jump in Latino turnout driven by opposition to Trump. With the 2016 presidential race in its final hours, the two candidates are making a last-minute sprint through swing states such as Florida, Pennsylvania and North Carolina. They have also headed north to Michigan and New Hampshire, states that Democrats have carried in recent cycles but that could flip this year. Here are the key states and signals to watch as the night goes on: Most realistic routes to victory for Trump begin with keeping two battlegrounds that Mitt Romney won four years ago, North Carolina and Arizona, and flipping three states that President Barack Obama won: Florida, Ohio and Iowa. Losing any of those states would seriously complicate Trump's already shaky path to 270 electoral votes. However, if Trump won back Pennsylvania or Michigan from the Democrats, who have carried both electoral-rich states six times in a row, North Carolina would become more expendable. Winning a state like Pennsylvania or Michigan would let Trump make up for losing North Carolina and still have a chance of reaching 270. If that does not happen, holding North Carolina and Arizona while taking back Florida, Ohio and Iowa from the Democrats, plus Maine's 2nd District, would only bring him to 260. Trump would then need to find 10 more electoral votes somewhere. New Hampshire's four and Nevada's six would get him there. Colorado, with nine electoral votes, Michigan with 15 and Pennsylvania with 20 are other possibilities. In his final 48 hours before Election Day, Trump has been just about everywhere, including Colorado, Michigan and even Minnesota, hunting for the extra votes he needs.

title: Study: Phytochemical In Broccoli And Cauliflower Goes After Prostate Cancer Cells
text: We all know we should eat our vegetables. At least, that is what most of us have been hearing since we were kids. What our mothers told us when we were young, our doctors tell us as we get older. Sometimes, though, it helps to have a more specific reason than high cholesterol, or even a motherly “because I said so.” Especially for those who aren’t big fans of eating organic greens. A study carried out at Oregon State University’s Linus Pauling Micronutrient Research Institute confirms that sulforaphane, a phytochemical found in broccoli and related cruciferous vegetables such as cauliflower and cabbage, has a natural ability to target and attack prostate cancer cells without harming the cells next to them. Unconnected studies suggest it may hold similar promise for breast cancer. The active chemicals in everyday foods such as broccoli are often far more potent than people would think. In fact, working out how to safely adapt these chemical ingredients for medical use is one of the biggest hurdles researchers face. Even edible plants considered “rich” in a particular nutritional substance contain relatively small amounts of it by volume. Most of these compounds can also become toxic to humans if taken in high enough concentrations. While a number of earlier investigations have proven that sulforaphane can attack both benign and malignant cancer cells, the Oregon State study is one of the first to prove that it works without disrupting otherwise healthy tissue. This hands researchers a tremendous tool for developing new, low-risk treatment options, and is likely to spur more research into the healing potential of other seemingly mundane edible plants.

title: Factbox: Comparing the Senate and House Obamacare overhaul bills
text: After weeks of closed-door talks, the U.S. Senate on Thursday released a draft of its healthcare bill, which would overhaul the Affordable Care Act, widely known as Obamacare. The House of Representatives narrowly approved its own healthcare bill last month. If the Senate passes its bill, the House will either have to vote on the Senate’s version of the legislation or the two chambers will have to resolve their differences in a conference committee. Obamacare extended coverage to some 20 million more Americans through a combination of subsidized private insurance and an expansion of Medicaid. Since the law was passed in 2010, Republicans have campaigned on repealing it, arguing that it is too expensive and amounts to undue government interference in Americans’ healthcare. Here is how the two bills compare on their main provisions: Under Obamacare, more than 30 states, about a dozen of them with Republican governors, expanded Medicaid, the government health insurance program for the poor and disabled. Both bills would reverse the expansion and substantially overhaul the program, which insures nearly 70 million people. SENATE: The draft would phase out Obamacare’s Medicaid expansion over three years, from 2021 to 2024. Beginning in 2025, it would then overhaul the program and cut its federal funding by more than the House bill would. HOUSE: The bill would let the Medicaid expansion continue until Jan. 1, 2020. After that, the expansion would end, and people enrolled under it could not re-enroll once they leave. Medicaid funding would be capped per person. SENATE: The bill would repeal most Obamacare taxes starting after Dec. 31, 2016, including the 3.8 percent net investment income tax on wealthy Americans.

title: New U.N. climate chief seeks fast action, at odds with Trump
text: The incoming climate chief of the United Nations said on Thursday that she will push for rapid action under a U.N. accord to slow global warming, and voiced hope that U.S. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump will drop his calls for a renegotiation if he is elected. Mexico’s Patricia Espinosa, a former foreign minister named on Wednesday to lead the Bonn-based U.N. Climate Change Secretariat from July, urged all governments to quickly ratify the 195-nation accord agreed in Paris in December. She said “it’s not impossible” that the agreement, which seeks to shift the global economy away from fossil fuels this century, could enter into force as soon as this year, giving it weight in international law. Espinosa is at odds with Trump, who doubts that man-made emissions cause climate change. Trump said on Tuesday that he was “not a big fan” of the Paris accord and that “at a minimum I will be renegotiating those agreements”. Asked about Trump’s threat, Espinosa said the Paris deal was a hard-won compromise among more than 190 nations. “It would not be easy for anybody to just say ‘I want to renegotiate this’,” she said. The nations that agreed in Paris range from the top greenhouse gas emitters, China and the United States, to small island nations afraid of rising sea levels and OPEC members that rely on oil income. Renegotiation “is really not a scenario that in a multilateral process you can see as something feasible,” she added. Espinosa said she would be “respectful of everybody who has a role to play in any country” while at the same time trying to build momentum for action. Many other supporters of the accord have expressed dismay at Trump’s call.
